q: Lay out Marsala's classification in full: colour, sweetness and ageing.
accept: oro ambra and rubino by colour secco semisecco and dolce by sugar and fine superiore riserva vergine and stravecchio by age
three colours three sweetness levels and five ageing categories from one year to ten
fine one year superiore two superiore riserva four vergine five vergine stravecchio ten
colour from the grapes sweetness in grams per litre and marsala ageing tiers up to a decade
ans: Three colours: Oro and Ambra from white grapes - Grillo, Catarratto, Inzolia (Ansonica) and Damaschino - and Rubino from at least 70% dark-skinned grapes, chiefly Perricone (Pignatello), Nero d'Avola and Nerello Mascalese, with white varieties permitted for the balance. Three sweetness classes: secco below 40 g/L, semisecco between 40 and 100, dolce above 100. Five ageing categories: Fine at one year, Superiore at two, Superiore Riserva at four, Vergine (also labelled Soleras) at five, and Vergine Stravecchio or Vergine Riserva at ten. Minimum total alcohol is 17.5% for Fine and 18% for everything above it, Superiore and Vergine alike. Ambra takes its colour from mosto cotto, which is permitted in no other category, and Vergine takes no sweetening agent at all - no mosto cotto, no sifone, no concentrated must - which is why it is the category serious producers work in.
exp: Marsala was invented for export by John Woodhouse in 1773 and destroyed by its own success as a cooking ingredient; the categories above are how you separate the two. Florio's Vergine and Marco De Bartoli's work are the argument that the wine belongs on a list rather than in a pan. Fix the two sweetening agents by name - they are what the Vergine category is defined against.

q: Explain the Saint-Émilion classification's revision cycle, and what happened at the 2022 revision.
accept: revised each decade and in 2022 ausone cheval blanc and angelus withdrew leaving figeac and pavie
estates opted out over the criteria and figeac joined pavie as premier grand cru classe a
a ten year cycle that can demote so it is repeatedly litigated
the 2022 edition lost its biggest names and promoted figeac
ans: It is revised roughly every ten years, it classifies the château rather than the land, estates must apply to be considered, and rank can be lost — which is what makes it unlike 1855 and what keeps it in court. The 2006 edition was annulled after litigation from demoted properties. Ahead of the 2022 revision, Ausone and Cheval Blanc announced in 2021 that they would not enter, objecting that the criteria weighted reputation, marketing, tourism and communication alongside the wine in the glass; Angélus withdrew soon after. That removed three of the four Premier Grand Cru Classé A estates. The classification that emerged promoted Figeac to join Pavie at the top tier, so the summit now holds two names, and the interesting question is whether a classification the greatest estates decline to enter still classifies anything.
exp: The general principle is worth stating aloud: a classification that can demote is a classification that will be sued, and the defensive response — auditable criteria covering tourism, environment and communication — is exactly what drove the top estates out. Compare the Cru Bourgeois solution, which is to make the ranking expire for everyone.

q: A low-sulfur cider smells clean, but leaves a stale popcorn and cage aftertaste some seconds after you swallow. Diagnose it and explain the mechanism.
accept: mousiness from tetrahydropyridines produced by brettanomyces and lactic bacteria
mousy taint perceived only retronasally because saliva raises the ph and volatilises it
mouse taint from low sulfur high ph ciders not fixable and worsens in bottle
ans: Mousiness. The compounds are nitrogen heterocycles — 2-acetyltetrahydropyridine, 2-ethyltetrahydropyridine and 2-acetylpyrroline — formed from lysine and ethanol by Brettanomyces and by lactic acid bacteria including Lactobacillus and Oenococcus. The reason the nose is clean is chemistry: at cider and wine pH these compounds are protonated and effectively non-volatile, so they cannot reach the olfactory epithelium from the glass. In the mouth, saliva at around pH 7 deprotonates them, they volatilise, and they arrive retronasally several seconds after the swallow as a long, stale, corn-chip or rodent-cage finish. Individual saliva pH varies, so a portion of any panel genuinely cannot perceive it, which is why arguments about mousiness get heated. To confirm, rub a drop on the back of a clean hand, let it warm, and smell; or simply wait through the finish. It is a spoilage fault, it intensifies with oxygen exposure and time in bottle, and it cannot be removed. The causes are the conditions that let those organisms work: little or no free SO2, high pH, oxygen ingress, and residual sugar or nutrients left in the finished drink — which is why it has become the signature fault of low-intervention cider and natural wine.
exp: This tests the one fault whose detection method is not sniffing the glass, and a Master should be able to explain both the pH mechanism and the taster variability it produces. The service consequence is practical: a guest may reject a bottle you cannot smell, and they may be right. Prevention is unglamorous and absolute — free SO2, pH discipline, oxygen control and a genuinely dry finish.

q: Explain the mechanisms by which a large body of water moderates a vineyard, and name three regions where the effect decides what can be planted.
accept: thermal inertia delays budbreak and extends autumn plus freeze protection breeze and light reflection
water lags air temperature moderating frost and winter lows finger lakes niagara and the mosel
heat storage frost protection air movement and reflection off the water
ans: Four mechanisms. First, thermal inertia: water warms and cools far more slowly than land, so a deep lake or sea lags the air, keeping spring cool — delaying budbreak past the frost window — and autumn warm, extending hang time into October and November. Second, freeze protection: a large body of unfrozen water keeps winter minima above the temperature that kills vine trunks, and where it does freeze, lake-effect snow insulates the root zone. Third, air movement: the land-water thermal gradient generates breeze that breaks up radiation frost, dries the canopy and lowers disease pressure — and in some places delivers cold fog instead, which is a different kind of moderation. Fourth, reflection of light onto slopes rising from the shore, which matters at high latitude where the sun is low. Cases where it is the whole argument: the Finger Lakes, where Riesling survives on slopes directly above Seneca and Cayuga — both well over 100 metres deep — and freezes out on the flats between them; the Niagara Peninsula and Michigan's lakeshore, where the lake plus escarpment circulation is the only reason vinifera is viable; and the Mosel and Rhine themselves, where the river's stored warmth and reflection off the water onto steep slate is part of why grapes ripen at 50 degrees north. Add Lake Garda for Bardolino and Lugana, Lake Constance for the Bodensee, Germany's southernmost and highest vineyards, and the Ciron and Garonne at Sauternes as a case where the water body delivers fog rather than heat.
exp: Depth and volume matter more than surface area, and saying so is the mark of a real answer — a shallow lake freezes over and stops working exactly when it is needed. Two-part warning to include: the same water that saves you from frost can shorten ripening by cooling summer, and coastal moderation often arrives as fog, which cuts radiation as well as heat.
